fact: In the foreword to the Ministry of Health's 2024-25 sector performance report the Minister of Health calls DHIS2 the ministry's official national health information platform, says the report is based on data captured in it, and urges stakeholders to rely on it and avoid parallel data platforms; the foreword is undated, so the published date is used.

The WHO and Ministry of Health maturity assessment states that DHIS 2 is implemented at national and sub-national/district levels, with integration of health programme data into it still in progress and routine report completeness at 62% (indicator data 57%); the brief is dated February 2025.

The WHO and Ministry of Health self-assessment scores strategic planning for the health information system at 13% and HIS financing at 7%, and lists an HIS policy, a strategic plan for HIS and financing for HIS among components still to be established; the brief is dated February 2025.

WHO reports that the first national DHIS2 audit, held in 2025, found 44.3% reporting completeness and 37.3% timeliness and led to a Technical Roadmap to merge duplicate datasets, correct indicator formulas and improve data structures.

WHO reports that in the third quarter of 2025 six national HMIS tools, the drug dispensing registers and monthly reporting vouchers for hospitals, PHCCs and PHCUs, were validated, approved and configured in DHIS2 with harmonised coding, and that EWARS was linked with DHIS2 and PLMIS.

WHO states that monthly reporting vouchers for hospitals, primary health care centres (PHCCs) and primary health care units (PHCUs) are configured in DHIS2 as of the third quarter of 2025; it does not say at which level they are keyed.

WHO reports that the Minister of Health names DHIS2 as South Sudan's national health information system and urges partners to report through it rather than parallel systems, and that technical working groups coordinate the HIS nationally and at state level under a DHIS2 support framework, which WHO calls government-led.

WHO reports that the 2025 national DHIS2 audit guided a Technical Roadmap for fixing DHIS2 (merging duplicate datasets, correcting indicator formulas, improving data structures); no cost or period is given.

The Ministry of Health reports that 30% of health facilities report directly through DHIS2 in 2025, against an HSSP target of 55%, these being the facilities equipped with tablets and computers; the share is of all health facilities and no numerator or denominator is given, and completeness of the OPD and inpatient form (MOH F01A) in DHIS2 was 52.15% in 2024/25.

The Ministry of Health reports that in 2025 the 30% of health facilities equipped with tablets and computers enter their own reports directly in DHIS2, and that facilities providing TB and HIV services were given tablets and data bundles to do so.

The Ministry of Health states that hospitals and PHCCs often lack the computers, stable internet and trained staff to enter data directly into DHIS2, so that data entry is frequently centralised or delayed; it does not name the level at which the entry is done (FY 2024/25).

The Ministry of Health's assessment of health service institutions finds that many hospitals submit DHIS2 reports regularly and that DHIS2 reporting is common among them, with monthly reporting and verification inconsistent in some and internal data tools not yet linked (FY 2024/25).

The Minister of Health calls DHIS2 the official national health information platform and asks all stakeholders to avoid parallel platforms; in FY 2024/25 the ministry operationalised a monthly M&E Technical Working Group and wrote a Data Governance Framework into its HMIS SOPs.

The Health Sector Strategic Plan 2023-2027 sets targets for the proportion of health facilities reporting directly through DHIS2 of 55% by 2025 and 90% by 2027, as the Ministry of Health's report tabulates them; the same report records a HIS maturity score of 13% for strategic planning and 7% for HIS financing.

The Ministry of Health reports that in FY 2024/25 ICT hardware, solar power and Starlink connectivity were deployed to selected health facilities, a facility data clean-up validated about 70% of facilities in DHIS2 as the master facility list, and over 500 facilities were matched between DHIS2 and EWARS.

The World Bank's mid-term review mission of 27 October to 14 November 2025 records that the M&E technical working group for HMIS integration was revitalised, HMIS SOPs and revised tools were being finalised and customised in DHIS2, and facilities in DHIS2 were verified with State Ministries of Health and closed or non-existent ones removed, raising completeness for forms such as OPD and malaria.

The project's results framework gives completeness of reporting by facilities as 58% for July 2024 to September 2025 against a 41% baseline and a 60% year-one target, rated constrained; reporting rates among HSTP-supported facilities are put above 85%.

The World Bank records HMIS strengthening as subcomponent 2.4 of the Health Sector Transformation Project, financed by IDA grants and a multi-donor trust fund and implemented by WHO, with UNDP/Global Fund and UNICEF also funding HMIS activities and the printing of HMIS tools; the government's US$8 million counterpart funding had not been deposited.
The World Bank names a Ministry of Health HMIS department and a Department of M&E as the counterparts for DHIS2 and the HMIS tools, with WHO carrying out the strengthening work under the project.

The Ministry of Health's Director General for Policy, Planning, Budget, Research, Monitoring and Evaluation names DHIS2 as the national health information system from which the abstract's routine service delivery, morbidity and mortality data are drawn; the statement is undated and is given the document's publication date.

The abstract, by the Ministry of Health and the National Bureau of Statistics, puts average DHIS2 reporting completeness at an estimated 60% over 2021 to 2024, with the national reporting rate for the OPD and inpatient form (MOH F01A) staying in the mid-60 per cent range and on-time reporting in the low 50s across the four years; DHIS2 indicators were adjusted from county level, where data were most complete, and stronger data entry at facility level is recommended.

WHO reports that in 2023 it supported the Ministry of Health to develop a five-year health information policy and strategy to guide implementation of the HMIS, and a five-year implementation roadmap setting out milestones, activities and resources for the country's health information systems; neither is said to be costed or adopted.

WHO describes the HMIS as the Ministry of Health's national health information system, to be strengthened by integrating other data collection and reporting systems into DHIS2, and says in 2023 that it is weakened by parallel systems run by implementing partners and short of skilled personnel to manage it.

A UNDP consultancy notice states that DHIS2, the Ministry of Health's electronic health information management system since 2018, has been scaled up to all counties and to some selected health facilities; the notice is undated and the fact is given its publication date.
The UNDP notice says DHIS2 reaches some selected health facilities besides all counties, and gives no number or share of facilities; the notice is undated and the fact is given its publication date.

The UNDP notice states that the Ministry of Health has used DHIS2 as South Sudan's electronic health information management system since 2018 and has a DHIS2 technical team, and that an HIS roadmap/plan was still to be reviewed and finalised; the notice is undated and the fact is given its publication date.

The World Bank brief states that the Ministry of Health, as steward of the health system, wants all reporting and monitoring organised under DHIS2 and is prioritising its rollout, with county health departments designated as the linchpins and in overall charge of DHIS2 reporting; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that respondents credited the Ministry of Health with articulating a clear strategy encouraging all facilities to report data to DHIS2, while some doubted its capacity to oversee the rollout; the strategy document is not named; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that health monitoring activities, of which HMIS including DHIS2 is one of three categories, are highly dependent on donor funding, raising concern for their sustainability once donor support is withdrawn; the statement is about monitoring as a whole and not DHIS2 alone; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that facility workers transmit their data to county health departments, which are in overall charge of DHIS2 reporting, that the system is web based, and that piloting facility-based DHIS2 at a handful of facilities such as busy hospitals was still only a recommendation to explore; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that the DHIS2 implementation was accelerating but had yet to involve a significant fraction, which it puts at 20 percent or more, of the country's health facilities; no numerator or denominator is given, and the figure is of facilities whose data reaches the system, not of clinics keying their own; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that county health departments are intended to be the focal point for DHIS2 data entry and uploading, and that some of them struggle with internet access and have no regular wifi or cellular network; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief states that most primary health care units and many primary health care centres lack computers or tablets for entering data, quotes a respondent that it is too early to introduce facility-level reporting and that tablets had been tried with many challenges, and lists facility-based DHIS2 data entry in high-volume facilities only as a pilot still to be done; no count is given; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The World Bank brief's table of technologies in use for health monitoring names the Ministry of Health as the user of DHIS2, with an offline data entry tool available for settings without internet; from interviews held September 2020 to March 2021.

The Ministry of Health's poster for the Health Data Collaborative, of November 2023, lists a five-year (2023-2028) health sector strategic plan and policy for the health information system and a five-year HMIS integration and interoperability roadmap, with efforts ongoing to roll DHIS2 out at county and health facility level.

A World Bank policy brief states that the Ministry of Health rolled DHIS2 out in 2018-2019 at county health department level by design, facility health workers handing in hand-written monthly reports that a county health official enters; no date is given for the account, so the document's year is used.
